exam: What bedside tests would you use to confirm RP in a clinic without ERG? — Confrontation visual fields, history of night blindness, and ophthalmoscopic bone‑spicule pigment.
How does RP differ from vitamin A deficiency on examination? — RP shows progressive field loss with pigmentary changes; deficiency improves with supplementation and lacks bone‑spicule pigment.
A child with RP develops central vision loss; what complication should you suspect? — Cystoid macular edema; consider acetazolamide if available.
Explain why high‑dose vitamin A is contraindicated in a patient with liver disease. — Vitamin A is hepatotoxic; liver disease increases risk of toxicity.

In a low‑resource setting, how would you counsel a family about inheritance when genetic testing is unavailable? — Use pedigree analysis to explain autosomal recessive/dominant patterns and recurrence risk.
What red‑flag symptom requires urgent referral from a patient with RP? — Sudden central vision loss or acute eye pain suggesting glaucoma.
Why might an early ERG be normal in RP, and how does this affect your diagnostic approach? — Rod loss may be subtle early; rely on clinical signs and history.
What low‑vision aid would you prioritize for a teenager with mid‑stage RP? — Telescopic glasses to enlarge distant images for school.
ai.title: Retinitis Pigmentosa
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited retinal dystrophies causing progressive photoreceptor loss. Diagnosis relies on clinical signs and simple tests, often without advanced imaging in low‑resource settings.

b: Diagnosis requires night‑blindness history, peripheral field constriction, and characteristic fundus changes.
Fundus: bone‑spicule pigment, attenuated vessels, optic disc pallor.
sections.p: RP is a hereditary degeneration of the retinal photoreceptors, beginning with rods and later affecting cones, leading to night blindness and peripheral visual field loss.

t.b: Confirms night blindness and field loss; distinguishes RP from cataract or refractive error.
Identifies bone‑spicule pigment and vessel attenuation; if unavailable, note reduced peripheral vision and normal anterior segment.
Shows reduced rod response early; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture.

b: Early: night blindness, normal visual acuity.
Mid: visual field <20°, mild acuity drop.
Late: visual acuity <6/60, central scotoma.
sections.p: Staging follows functional vision loss: early (night blindness), mid (constricted fields), late (central vision loss).

b: Autosomal recessive genes (e.g., USH2A, RPE65).
Autosomal dominant genes (e.g., RHO).
X‑linked (RPGR).
Syndromic associations: NARP, Usher syndrome.
sections.p: RP is genetically heterogeneous; autosomal recessive forms are common in consanguineous African families.

b: Night blindness before age 10.
Gradual peripheral field constriction.
Preserved central acuity until late stage.
sections.p: Children often present with difficulty seeing at dusk, bumping into objects, and progressive loss of peripheral vision.

b: Fundus photography if available for documentation.
ERG to quantify rod vs cone loss.
sections.p: In low‑resource settings focus on bedside tools; refer for genetic testing only when it will change management.

t.b: Detects peripheral field loss; if unavailable, ask patient to describe side‑by‑side object detection.
Identifies specific mutation for counseling; if unavailable, provide family risk counseling based on inheritance pattern.

b: Rapid central vision decline → macular edema.
Lens opacities → cataract.
Elevated intra‑ocular pressure → glaucoma.
sections.p: Complications include cystoid macular edema, cataract, and secondary glaucoma; sudden vision loss warrants urgent review.

b: Low‑vision aids (magnifiers, telescopes).
Vitamin A 15 000 IU/day only in non‑pregnant patients with normal liver function; avoid in liver disease.
Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide) for cystoid macular edema when available.
Counseling on mobility and education.
sections.p: No cure; management aims to preserve vision, treat complications, and support psychosocial needs.

b: Track field constriction with confrontation testing.
Screen for cataract and glaucoma annually.
Provide information on inheritance and reproductive options.
sections.p: Regular 6‑monthly reviews to monitor visual fields, cataract development, and macular edema; genetic counseling for families.

Congenital stationary night blindness – non‑progressive.
Chronic retinal detachment – acute visual field loss.
sections.p: Conditions that cause night blindness or peripheral field loss can mimic RP.

Absence of bone‑spicule pigment early → do not rule out RP.
sections.p: Early ERG may be normal despite symptoms; fundus may appear unremarkable in very early disease.
